newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: U.N. drive for action on corruption gathers pace.
newsitem.headline: U.N. drive for action on corruption gathers pace.

text.p: Growing corruption of public officials threatens to undermine democracy and international trade worldwide, but more governments were taking steps to improve their accountability, U.N. officials said on Wednesday.

Dimitrios Vlassis, a U.N. Commission on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice official, told a news briefing that support among member states for a U.N.-led drive to battle corruption had risen dramatically.
"As transparency becomes the norm rather than the exception, corruption becomes a problem that affects democratic institutions and creates inequalities," Vlassis said.
"We are receiving more and more requests from countries for assistance with this problem," he noted.
The issue of corruption is high on the agenda of the commission's sixth session, which is due to end on Friday.
In December, the General Assembly adopted two resolutions setting down guidelines for a code of conduct for public officials and a convention on bribery in international trade.

"We need to speed up action to implement the commitments made at the General Assembly in December," Jonathon Weiner, U.S. deputy assistant secretary of state in the bureau of international narcotics and law enforcement, told Reuters.
"Officials are to a country what white blood cells are to the body. They are its defence against the disease of crime and corrupt payments are like carcinogenics," he said.
Weiner noted that the United States was particularly concerned about the practice of treating bribes to foreign officials as a tax-deductible expense.
"In a globalised world it should not be permitted for any country to have a practice where it's okay to bribe to gain contracts. It is unacceptable," he said.
In Germany, Britain and France, bribing officials in countries where corruption is rampant is considered to be acceptable, said a Western delegate who declined to be named.
Another problem area being discussed by the commission was the abuse of the immunity of senior officials.
The delegate said that the problem was especially pronounced in Russia, where no judge can be investigated without the approval of all other judges.
The U.N. has already organised a seminar on corruption for police and prosecutors in Central and Eastern European countries and plans to hold a second seminar early next year.
A meeting of African ministers in Senegal is also planned in the next few months to discuss international cooperation in the fight against corruption.
